etymology: From the Old English tannian, “to tan,” through the Medieval Latin tannare, from tannum, the crushed oak bark whose liquor cures hide into leather; hence one whose trade is the dressing of the skins of dead beasts.
biblical_def: A tanner is the workman who takes the raw skin of a dead beast and turns it into leather — soaking, scraping, liming, and steeping it in bark liquor until the hide will neither rot nor stiffen. It is a stinking trade, and under the law it was worse than stinking: the man who handled a carcase was ceremonially defiled, for “he that toucheth the carcase thereof shall be unclean until the even” (Lev 11:39). A tannery therefore stood outside the town, downwind, and by the water; and Scripture notes the very address: Peter “tarried many days in Joppa with one Simon a tanner” (Act 9:43), whose “house is by the sea side” (Act 10:6). The Holy Ghost did not hide the trade or apologise for it. He recorded it twice more, as though the lodging were part of the sermon. And it was. For it is in that house, on that roof, over that smell, that Peter is given the sheet let down from heaven and the word, “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” (Act 10:15). The apostle who would be sent to a Gentile centurion was first lodged with a man whose honest labour left him ceremonially unclean, and he learned there to say, “God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean” (Act 10:28). The trade nobody wanted became the schoolroom where the gospel went to the nations.
webster_summary: One whose occupation is to tan hides, or convert them into leather by steeping in bark liquor.
webster_full: TANNER, one whose occupation is to tan hides, or convert them into leather by means of tannin.
From the Old English tannian, through Medieval Latin tannare, from tannum, oak bark.
The work required carcases, lime, and running water, and so was set outside the city.
Peter lodged with Simon a tanner at Joppa, by the sea side (Act 9:43; Act 10:6).
Under the ceremonial law the handling of dead beasts rendered a man unclean until the even (Lev 11:39).
scriptures: Act 9:43
And it came to pass, that he tarried many days in Joppa with one Simon a tanner.
Act 10:6
He lodgeth with one Simon a tanner, whose house is by the sea side: he shall tell thee what thou oughtest to do.
And if any beast, of which ye may eat, die; he that toucheth the carcase thereof shall be unclean until the even.

And he said unto them, Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.
corruption_summary: The old error made the tanner a second-class saint; the new error makes every man's job the measure of his worth.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome built a two-storey Christianity: the cloister above, the workshop below; the monk pursuing the counsels of perfection, the tanner permitted a lower and grubbier salvation. The Reformers tore the staircase down. Luther and Calvin alike insisted that the milkmaid at her pail and the tanner at his pit serve God in a calling as truly holy as the preacher in his pulpit, because holiness is not in the smell of the work but in the faith and obedience of the worker. The Spirit’s own record vindicates them. He does not name Simon of Joppa as a man to be pitied for his employment; He names the trade plainly, three times, and sets the house by the sea down in the middle of the book of Acts as the place where God broke open the door to the Gentiles. No trade is too common for the Lord to lodge in.

The modern corruption runs the opposite way and is no better. Our age has made work the source of identity rather than a station of service: a man is now what his business card says, and the trades that soil the hands are despised by the very culture that cannot live a week without them. Scripture will not have it. The Fourth Commandment presumes six days of labour as well as one of rest; Paul commands the converted thief to labour “working with his hands the thing which is good” (Eph 4:28); and the same apostle who wrought with leather and goats’ hair felt no shame in it. The tanner’s answer to both errors is the same: he is not saved by his trade and he is not defined by it, but he glorifies God in it.
roots_summary: A dresser of hides; a ceremonially defiling trade honoured by God in the record of Acts.
roots_lines: Tanner — from Old English tannian, to cure hide with oak-bark liquor.
The trade required dead beasts, and so ceremonial uncleanness (Lev 11:39).
Tanneries stood outside the town and beside water — hence “by the sea side” (Act 10:6).
Simon of Joppa is twice named a tanner without apology (Act 9:43; Act 10:6).
In that house Peter saw the sheet and heard, What God hath cleansed, call not common (Act 10:15).
usage: Peter lodged with a tanner — and the Spirit thought the address worth recording.
The tanner’s trade made him unclean by the law; it never made him unclean before grace.
No man’s calling is too low to be a station of obedience.

etymology: From the Old English dēagian, “to dye,” from dēag, a colour or hue; hence one whose trade is to fix colour permanently into cloth, wool, skin, or thread.
biblical_def: A dyer is the craftsman who drives colour into a fabric until the colour is no longer on the cloth but in it. Scripture does not use the noun, but the trade is everywhere in its pages and its ordinances. The tabernacle covering required “rams’ skins dyed red” (Exo 25:5); the priestly hangings demanded blue, purple, and scarlet, each of them a costly dyer’s work; and Lydia of Thyatira, the first convert named in Europe, was “a seller of purple” (Act 16:14) from a city whose guilds were famous for the vats. Her trade was lawful, profitable, and no barrier whatever to grace: while she heard Paul, “whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken” (Act 16:14). The prophets seize the picture for the LORD Himself. Who is this that cometh “with dyed garments from Bozrah” (Isa 63:1)? It is the Redeemer, whose raiment is stained not with madder or murex but with the blood of judgment, “mighty to save.” And the last book turns the dye-vat inside out: the saints are they which “have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev 7:14). Every earthly dye darkens the cloth; this one alone whitens it. The dyer’s art can fix a colour for a lifetime; the blood of Christ fixes a righteousness for ever.
webster_summary: One whose occupation is to dye cloth and the like; one who fixes colours permanently into fabric.
webster_full: DYER, one whose occupation is to dye cloth, wool, or thread; a colourer of fabrics.
From Old English dēagian, to dye, from dēag, colour or hue.
The ancient dyes were costly: murex purple, kermes scarlet, madder red, woad and indigo blue.
Rams’ skins dyed red covered the tabernacle (Exo 25:5); blue, purple, and scarlet clothed its hangings.
Lydia of Thyatira traded in purple and was the first named convert in Europe (Act 16:14).
scriptures: Exo 25:5
And rams' skins dyed red, and badgers' skins, and shittim wood,
And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.
Isa 63:1
Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength? I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save.
Rev 7:14
And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
corruption_summary: A lawful trade in beauty — and a standing rebuke to the notion that commerce and conversion cannot dwell in one house.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God gives colour, and that the making and selling of beautiful things is an honourable calling under Him. Two errors stand on either side of the road. The first is the ascetic instinct that suspects beauty as such, as though a drab world were a holier one; but the LORD Himself prescribed blue, purple, and scarlet for His sanctuary and clothed His priests in glory and beauty. The second is the merchant’s instinct that reduces beauty to inventory and the customer to a margin. Lydia stands between them: a woman of substance in a luxury trade whose heart the Lord opened, and whose first act after baptism was to fling her house open to the preachers (Act 16:15).

There is a caution in the dye-vat as well. The whole art of the dyer is to make an outside look like something it is not by nature — wool is not purple; the vat makes it so. Religion attempts the same trick when it dyes the outside of a man and leaves the heart its old colour, and the LORD rebukes that trade in every age: whited walls, painted sepulchres, garments changed while the nature is not. The only dye that reaches the man himself comes from Calvary, and it runs the wrong way for the natural mind: “though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isa 1:18). Christ does not tint the sinner; He makes him new.
roots_summary: One who fixes colour into cloth; the trade behind the tabernacle's blue, purple, and scarlet.
roots_lines: Dyer — Old English dēagian, to dye, from dēag, a colour.
The noun is absent from the Authorized Version, but the trade fills the Levitical ordinances.
Rams’ skins dyed red covered the tabernacle (Exo 25:5).
Lydia sold purple at Philippi and was converted there (Act 16:14).
The LORD comes from Bozrah with dyed garments, mighty to save (Isa 63:1).
usage: The dyer fixes a colour; Christ fixes a righteousness.
Lydia’s purple never hindered her conversion, and her conversion never shamed her purple.
Every earthly dye darkens the cloth; the blood of the Lamb alone makes it white.

etymology: From the Latin fullo, a cloth-cleanser, through Old English fullere; the trade of scouring, thickening, and whitening newly woven cloth by treading it in a strong alkaline lye — hence the harsh “fullers’ soap” of Scripture.
biblical_def: A fuller is the launderer and finisher of cloth: he treads the new-woven web in a trough of nitre, lye, and stale urine, beats it, scours it, and lays it out in the sun until the natural grease and yellow are gone and the wool is white. It was heavy, foul-smelling, water-hungry work, done outside the walls; Jerusalem had its landmark “fuller’s field” where Isaiah met Ahaz (Isa 7:3). Two texts lift the trade into doctrine. Malachi asks who can endure the coming of the Lord, “for he is like a refiner’s fire, and like fullers’ soap” (Mal 3:2) — a double figure of purging: the fire that burns the dross out of metal, the caustic that scours the filth out of wool. The Messiah does not merely forgive the stain; He attacks it. Then, on the holy mount, Mark reaches for the fuller and finds him bankrupt: “his raiment became shining, exceeding white as snow; so as no fuller on earth can white them” (Mar 9:3). Here is the crown of the trade and the end of it. The best whiteness human labour can produce is not in the same order as the whiteness of Christ transfigured. All our scouring is comparative; His righteousness is absolute. Which is why the promise of pardon is put in exactly these terms: “though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isa 1:18) — not by our trough, but by His blood.
webster_summary: One whose occupation is to full cloth — to scour, cleanse, and whiten it after weaving.
webster_full: FULLER, one whose occupation is to full cloth; a cleanser and thickener of woollen webs.
From Latin fullo, a cloth-cleanser, through Old English fullere.
The work used strong alkalies — nitre, lye, and fullers’ earth — hence “fullers’ soap” (Mal 3:2).
It required much water and open ground, so the fuller’s field lay outside Jerusalem (Isa 7:3).
Mark measures the transfiguration against the trade: no fuller on earth could white them (Mar 9:3).
scriptures: Mal 3:2
But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap:
Mar 9:3
And his raiment became shining, exceeding white as snow; so as no fuller on earth can white them.
Isa 7:3
Then said the LORD unto Isaiah, Go forth now to meet Ahaz, thou, and Shearjashub thy son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field;
Isa 1:18
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
corruption_summary: The fuller's trough is the standing rebuke to every scheme of self-cleansing, ancient or modern.
corruption_paragraphs: The oldest corruption of this word is the belief that a man can full his own cloth. Rome institutionalised it — penance, satisfaction, the treasury of merit, purgatorial scouring after death — and every one of those is a fuller’s trough set up where only the blood of Christ can stand. Mark’s sentence on the mount ends the argument: no fuller on earth can white them. The whiteness of the transfigured Christ is not the top of a scale our labour climbs; it is a different order altogether, the outshining of His own essential holiness. What is imputed to the believer in justification is that righteousness and no other — Christ’s active obedience reckoned to him, not his own laundered attempts reckoned as good enough.

The modern version swaps the trough for the therapist’s couch and the self-improvement shelf. The stain is renamed a mistake, a wound, or a phase; the remedy is renamed growth; and the man scrubs at his own record hoping the yellow will fade. It never does. But note what Malachi joins to the soap: the refiner’s fire. God’s cleansing of His people is not a gentle rinse; it is caustic and it is hot, and it is aimed at sin rather than at the sinner’s comfort. That is mercy, not cruelty — the Lord who scours His church is the Lord who first bore her filth in His own body on the tree, and who will present her at last without spot.
roots_summary: A cloth-cleanser; the earthly trade whose best whiteness the transfiguration outran.
roots_lines: Fuller — Latin fullo, a cleanser of cloth; Old English fullere.
To full is to scour, thicken, and whiten newly woven wool.
“Fullers’ soap” names a caustic alkali, not a gentle wash (Mal 3:2).
The fuller’s field was a Jerusalem landmark outside the wall (Isa 7:3).
Christ’s raiment on the mount passed every fuller’s reach (Mar 9:3).
usage: Fullers’ soap is God’s figure for a cleansing that bites.
No fuller on earth can white them — the trade confesses its own limit.
Justification is not our cloth scoured whiter but Christ’s righteousness reckoned ours.

etymology: From the Old French maçon, a builder in stone, of Frankish origin; hence a worker who dresses, squares, and lays stone in wall or building.
biblical_def: A mason is a builder in stone — the man who quarries, hews, squares, and beds the stone that others will live behind. The Authorized Version names him in the sober company of carpenters and hewers, always at work on somebody’s house. When David was established, “Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, and carpenters, and masons: and they built David an house” (2Sa 5:11). When Joash gathered money to mend the temple, it went “to masons, and hewers of stone, and to buy timber and hewed stone to repair the breaches of the house of the LORD” (2Ki 12:12), and the account adds that the workmen dealt faithfully. When Jehoiada renewed the work, they “hired masons and carpenters to repair the house of the LORD” (2Ch 24:12). When the exiles returned, they “gave money also unto the masons, and to the carpenters” (Ezr 3:7). Notice the pattern: masons appear at every point where the house of God is built or repaired, and Scripture never once treats their wages as a lesser expense than the priests’ incense. The trade also gives the New Testament its great figure. There is a stone the builders refused, and it “is become the head stone of the corner” (Psa 118:22) — Christ Himself, rejected by the men whose whole business was to judge stone, and set by God as the corner on which the whole building rises.
webster_summary: One whose occupation is to lay stones or bricks; a builder of walls and stone-work.
webster_full: MASON, one whose occupation is to lay bricks and stones, or to construct the walls of buildings.
From Old French maçon, a stone-builder.
Scripture pairs him constantly with the carpenter and the hewer of stone.
Hiram’s masons built David’s house (2Sa 5:11); Joash’s masons repaired the LORD’s (2Ki 12:12).
The builders’ rejected stone became the head of the corner (Psa 118:22).
scriptures: And to masons, and hewers of stone, and to buy timber and hewed stone to repair the breaches of the house of the LORD, and for all that was laid out for the house to repair it.

And the king and Jehoiada gave it to such as did the work of the service of the house of the LORD, and hired masons and carpenters to repair the house of the LORD, and also such as wrought iron and brass to mend the house of the LORD.
Ezr 3:7

They gave money also unto the masons, and to the carpenters; and meat, and drink, and oil, unto them of Zidon, and to them of Tyre, to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea of Joppa, according to the grant that they had of Cyrus king of Persia.
The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.
corruption_summary: An honourable trade whose name was borrowed by a secret lodge with another gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: The plain corruption of this word is Freemasonry, which took the guild name and the working tools of an honest craft and hung upon them a religion. In the lodge the Great Architect is a deity vague enough to be affirmed by the Christian, the Jew, the Muslim, and the deist together; the candidate is made a brother by ceremony rather than by the new birth; the name of Christ is deliberately omitted from prayers so that no man be offended; and light, life, and hope are promised on terms that never mention His blood. That is not a fraternity beside the church, it is a rival cultus, and no confessional Reformed church can treat it as an indifferent society. The Second Commandment governs how God may be approached, and a worship stripped of the Mediator is not worship at all.

Under that lies a second and quieter error: the assumption that skilled hands are for hire but not for glory. Scripture will not separate the two. The masons of Joash worked on the house of the LORD, and the record commends them for dealing faithfully; the wages of the workman are named in the same breath as the service of the sanctuary. A Christian bricklayer who lays a true course to the line is doing something God notices — “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23). And every mason handles daily a parable he did not invent: the stone the builders refused. Men whose trade was judging stone rejected the only Stone that would bear the weight of the world.
roots_summary: A builder in stone; the trade that gave Scripture its figure of the rejected cornerstone.
roots_lines: Mason — Old French maçon, a worker in stone.
The AV names masons alongside carpenters and hewers of stone.
Tyre supplied David’s masons; Zidon and Tyre supplied the returning exiles’ (2Sa 5:11; Ezr 3:7).
Temple repair money went directly to masons’ wages (2Ki 12:12; 2Ch 24:12).
The builders’ refused stone is Christ, head of the corner (Psa 118:22).
usage: Masons appear wherever the house of God is built or repaired.
The trade that judges stone rejected the Chief Corner Stone.
A true course laid to the line is service rendered to the Lord.

etymology: From tent (Old French tente, from Latin tendere, “to stretch”) and maker; rendering the Greek skēnopoios, a worker in the coarse goats’-hair cloth and leather of which travellers’ tents were made.
biblical_def: A tentmaker cuts and stitches the heavy goats’-hair cloth called cilicium — the very fabric of Paul’s native Cilicia — into tents, awnings, and coverings. It is hard on the hands and it smells; and it is the trade the LORD gave the greatest missionary in the history of the church. Coming to Corinth, Paul found Aquila and Priscilla, “and because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers” (Act 18:3). He preached in the synagogue every sabbath and worked at the bench through the week. He was not ashamed to say so, holding up his hands before the Ephesian elders: “ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me” (Act 20:34). This was no denial of the minister’s right to support — Paul argues that right at length elsewhere — but a voluntary waiving of it, that no man might say he preached for hire. From the same conviction he laid down the rule for every congregation: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10), and pressed the quiet, unspectacular ideal: “that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11). The apostle to the Gentiles kept a needle and an awl, and the church has never been allowed to forget it.
webster_summary: One who makes tents; the trade of Paul, Aquila, and Priscilla at Corinth.
webster_full: TENTMAKER, one whose occupation is the making of tents from cloth or skins.
Rendering the Greek skēnopoios, a worker in goats’-hair cloth and leather.
The coarse cloth called cilicium took its name from Paul’s own province of Cilicia.
Paul, Aquila, and Priscilla shared the craft at Corinth (Act 18:3).
By it Paul supported himself and his company rather than burden the churches (Act 20:34).
scriptures: Act 18:3
And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.
Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me.
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
corruption_summary: Paul's awl rebukes two opposite errors: the hireling who preaches for gain, and the idler who will not work at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The first live corruption is the professionalised religion Paul deliberately refused to look like. There were teachers at Corinth and Crete alike who trafficked in doctrine “for filthy lucre’s sake” (Tit 1:11), and the modern platform has multiplied them: the conference circuit, the donation appeal timed to the emotional crescendo, the ministry whose books are its real business. The tentmaker is the standing answer. A man who can feed himself by his hands has removed the strongest temptation to trim his preaching, and the congregation that watches him stitch through the week knows exactly what his sermon is not for sale. Note carefully that Paul never denied the labourer his hire; he waived a right he had, which is a different and higher thing than pretending the right does not exist.

The opposite corruption is the idleness Paul had to rebuke in the same letter that gave us the rule. Some at Thessalonica were “working not at all, but are busybodies” (2Th 3:11), spiritualising their laziness with talk of the Lord’s return. The apostolic command is blunt and unfashionable: if a man will not work, let him not eat. This is not a denial of mercy to the widow, the orphan, the sick, or the man who cannot find work — Scripture is loud in their defence — but it is a refusal to subsidise the able-bodied unwilling. Between the hireling and the idler stands the tentmaker: a man who preaches for nothing and eats what his own hands have earned.
roots_summary: A maker of goats'-hair tents; Paul's trade and the model of self-supporting ministry.
roots_lines: Tentmaker — Greek skēnopoios, a worker in tent-cloth and leather.
Tent traces to Latin tendere, to stretch.
Cilician goats’-hair cloth was the standard material — Paul’s home industry.
At Corinth the craft joined Paul to Aquila and Priscilla (Act 18:3).
The bench funded the mission: these hands have ministered unto my necessities (Act 20:34).
usage: A tentmaking ministry is not a lesser ministry; it was the apostle’s own.
If any would not work, neither should he eat — apostolic, not merely proverbial.
Paul waived his right to support; he never denied that the right existed.

etymology: From silver (Old English seolfor) and smith (Old English smiþ, a worker in metal); rendering the Greek argurokopos, literally a beater of silver — one who works the metal into vessels, ornaments, and shrines.
biblical_def: A silversmith beats and casts silver into vessels and ornaments. The word occurs once in the Authorized Version, and it introduces one of the ugliest scenes in Acts: “a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen” (Act 19:24). Paul’s preaching at Ephesus had emptied the shops, and Demetrius called a guild meeting. Mark the order of his argument, for the Holy Ghost records it exactly. He begins with the money: “Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth” (Act 19:25). Then he states the doctrinal offence: Paul says “they be no gods, which are made with hands” (Act 19:26). Only afterwards does he reach for the piety, that the temple of the great goddess might be despised. The riot that followed cried Diana for two hours, but its engine was the till. Here is the trade’s whole warning. The metal is innocent; silver adorned the tabernacle and the temple. The corruption is a craft turned to manufacturing gods, and then a religion defended because it pays. Demetrius is the ancestor of every man who has ever loved a doctrine for its revenue, and he stands in Scripture as the case in point of Paul’s own verdict: “the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10).
webster_summary: One whose occupation is to work in silver; a beater and caster of silver vessels and ornaments.
webster_full: SILVERSMITH, one whose occupation is to work in silver, or to make silver vessels and ornaments.
From silver and smith, a worker in metal; Greek argurokopos, a beater of silver.
The word appears once in the Authorized Version, of Demetrius at Ephesus (Act 19:24).
He made silver shrines for Diana and brought no small gain to the craftsmen.
His plea to the guild began with wealth and only afterwards with the goddess (Act 19:25–27).
scriptures: For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith, which made silver shrines for Diana, brought no small gain unto the craftsmen;
Whom he called together with the workmen of like occupation, and said, Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth.
Moreover ye see and hear, that not alone at Ephesus, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul hath persuaded and turned away much people, saying that they be no gods, which are made with hands:
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
corruption_summary: Religion defended for profit's sake — Demetrius is the founding father of the prosperity racket.
corruption_paragraphs: “By this craft we have our wealth” is the confession beneath a great deal of religion. Rome perfected it in the indulgence trade that Tetzel hawked through Germany until Wittenberg answered him; and the trade never died, it only changed currency. The modern form is the prosperity gospel, in which the seed-faith offering is preached as the mechanism of blessing, the anointing is sold in bottles, and the ministry’s doctrine is shaped, quietly and unfalsifiably, by what raises money. Peter named the sin at its birth when Simon offered cash for the Spirit’s gift. Paul named it when he said some teach what they ought not for filthy lucre’s sake. Demetrius simply said it out loud, and Luke wrote it down so the church could recognise the voice.

The corruption is not the craft. Silver is a good creature of God, and the men who beat it for the tabernacle are honoured in Exodus. Two things spoil it. First, the object: shrines for Diana are graven images, and the Second Commandment binds the workman’s hands as surely as the worshipper’s knees. Second, the motive: a craft becomes a curse the moment its profits decide a man’s theology. The test is simple and searching. What would this doctrine cost me if it were true? Demetrius knew exactly what Paul’s doctrine would cost him — and he chose the till. Every generation must answer the same question with its own accounts open.
roots_summary: A worker in silver; named once, of Demetrius, whose piety was purchased by his profits.
roots_lines: Silversmith — silver + smith, Old English smiþ, a metal-worker.
Greek argurokopos, literally a beater of silver.
Its single AV occurrence names Demetrius of Ephesus (Act 19:24).
His shrines for Diana were graven images made with hands (Act 19:26).
The guild’s riot was piety in the mouth and profit in the purse (Act 19:25).
usage: By this craft we have our wealth — the oldest reason for defending a false religion.
The silversmith’s sin was not the silver but the shrine, and not the shrine but the till.
Demetrius is the ancestor of every ministry whose doctrine follows its donations.

etymology: From gold (Old English gold) and smith (Old English smiþ, a worker in metal); rendering Hebrew tsoreph, a refiner or founder — one who melts, refines, and overlays in gold.
biblical_def: A goldsmith refines the metal and works it: melting, casting, beating it thin, and overlaying wood or stone with plate. Scripture shows him in two opposite postures, and the contrast is the whole lesson. In Isaiah he is the idol-maker’s partner: “the workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold” (Isa 40:19); the carpenter cheers him on, and they nail the finished god down “that it should not be moved” (Isa 41:7) — a deity requiring carpentry to keep it upright. Isaiah drives it home elsewhere: men lavish gold out of the bag, “and hire a goldsmith; and he maketh it a god: they fall down, yea, they worship” (Isa 46:6). The prophet is not describing superstition among savages; he is describing an economy, a supply chain, a trade contracted to produce an object of worship. Then turn to Nehemiah. When the wall of Jerusalem lay in rubble, “next unto him repaired Uzziel the son of Harhaiah, of the goldsmiths” (Neh 3:8), and a goldsmith’s son took his own section too (Neh 3:31). Men whose hands were trained to fine, delicate, valuable work laid down the graver and picked up rubble to rebuild the city of God. Same trade, same skill, two masters. The goldsmith who serves an idol builds a god that must be fastened down; the goldsmith who serves the LORD helps rebuild a wall that stands.
webster_summary: One who works in gold — refining, casting, and overlaying; in Scripture both idol-maker and wall-builder.
webster_full: GOLDSMITH, one whose occupation is to manufacture vessels and ornaments of gold; a worker and refiner of gold.
From gold and smith; Hebrew tsoreph, a refiner or founder.
Isaiah repeatedly sets him at the idol-maker’s bench (Isa 40:19; Isa 41:7; Isa 46:6).
Nehemiah sets the goldsmiths on the broken wall of Jerusalem (Neh 3:8, 31).
The same skill serves a nailed-down idol or the city of God.
scriptures: The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold, and casteth silver chains.
Isa 41:7

So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, and he that smootheth with the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying, It is ready for the sodering: and he fastened it with nails, that it should not be moved.
Isa 46:6
They lavish gold out of the bag, and weigh silver in the balance, and hire a goldsmith; and he maketh it a god: they fall down, yea, they worship.
Neh 3:8
Next unto him repaired Uzziel the son of Harhaiah, of the goldsmiths. Next unto him also repaired Hananiah the son of one of the apothecaries, and they fortified Jerusalem unto the broad wall.
corruption_summary: A skill is never neutral: the same hands that gild an idol can rebuild a wall.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah’s irony is the sharpest treatment of idolatry in Scripture and it is aimed at a tradesman. A god is commissioned, costed, cast, gilded, and then nailed to the floor so it will not fall over. The prophet does not argue that the idol is powerless; he lets the manufacturing process argue it. And the modern reader should not congratulate himself on having outgrown the workshop. The idols of a gilded age are made in the same way — conceived by desire, financed out of the bag, fabricated by skilled professionals, and defended by everyone employed in their production. Whatever a man will spend himself to obtain, adorn, and prop upright is his god; the Second Commandment reaches the advertising studio as surely as the founder’s furnace.

The recovery is in Nehemiah 3. Uzziel of the goldsmiths, and Hananiah the son of one of the apothecaries, repaired the wall and fortified Jerusalem unto the broad wall. Neither man was a mason. Both left the fine bench for common labour because the city of God was in ruins and the work needed hands. That chapter is the sanest picture of vocation in the Old Testament: priests, perfumers, goldsmiths, merchants, and the daughters of Shallum, each with a named section, none of them despising the mortar. A man’s trade gives him tools and standing; it does not give him leave to sit down when the wall is broken.
roots_summary: A refiner and worker of gold; in Isaiah he gilds idols, in Nehemiah he rebuilds the wall.
roots_lines: Goldsmith — gold + smith, a worker in metal.
Hebrew tsoreph means a refiner or founder, one who smelts and purifies.
He overlays the graven image with plate (Isa 40:19).
The finished god must be nailed down lest it topple (Isa 41:7).
Goldsmiths repaired their own section of Jerusalem’s wall (Neh 3:8, 31).
usage: They hire a goldsmith, and he maketh it a god — idolatry as an industry.
A god that must be fastened with nails cannot fasten anything else.
The goldsmiths of Nehemiah 3 laid down the graver and took up the wall.

etymology: From the Old English wefan, “to weave,” akin to the German weben; hence one who interlaces warp and woof upon a loom to form cloth.
biblical_def: A weaver crosses thread over thread on the loom — the warp stretched, the woof driven through by the shuttle — until a garment stands where there was only yarn. Scripture takes three things from his bench. First, speed: “My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle, and are spent without hope” (Job 7:6). The shuttle flies so fast the eye cannot follow, and it is empty again before you have watched it cross. Second, the cutting-off. Hezekiah, sick to death, moans, “I have cut off like a weaver my life: he will cut me off with pining sickness” (Isa 38:12); the web is severed from the loom while the pattern is still unfinished, and the weaver who cuts it is God. The spear-staff of Goliath is likened to “a weaver’s beam” (1Sa 17:7), so heavy a beam that the giant’s pride wanted no other measure. But the third use is the crown. At the cross the soldiers parted the garments four ways, “and also his coat: now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout” (Joh 19:23). They would not tear it; they cast lots for it. Christ’s righteousness is a seamless robe — not stitched together out of pieces, not divisible, not to be had in part. A man receives all of it or none, and he receives it as a gift by lot, not by labour.
webster_summary: One whose occupation is to weave; one who forms cloth by interlacing warp and woof.
webster_full: WEAVER, one whose occupation is to weave; one who forms cloth by crossing threads on a loom.
From Old English wefan, to weave.
The shuttle carries the woof across the stretched warp — a figure of speed (Job 7:6).
The beam holds the warp; Goliath’s spear-staff was like a weaver’s beam (1Sa 17:7).
Christ’s coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout (Joh 19:23).
scriptures: Job 7:6
My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope.
Mine age is departed, and is removed from me as a shepherd's tent: I have cut off like a weaver my life: he will cut me off with pining sickness: from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me.
And the staff of his spear was like a weaver's beam; and his spear's head weighed six hundred shekels of iron: and one bearing a shield went before him.
Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments, and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also his coat: now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout.
corruption_summary: The shuttle preaches the shortness of life; the seamless coat forbids a patchwork righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: Job’s shuttle is the standing rebuke to the modern conceit that time is a resource to be optimised rather than a mercy to be accounted for. Our age fills its hours with more than any previous generation could and remembers less of them; a life measured in productivity is a web with no pattern in it. Scripture’s counsel is not to work less but to number better: “so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” (Psa 90:12). The weaver at the loom knows something the calendar-keeper forgets — that the cutting-off is not his to schedule. Hezekiah did not choose the day the web came off the beam, and neither will any reader of this page.

The seamless coat guards a doctrine. Woven from the top throughout, it could not be divided without being destroyed, and the soldiers who would gladly have quartered it cast lots instead. So it is with the righteousness of Christ. It is not pieced together from His merit and ours, not partly imputed and partly achieved, not a fabric to which sanctification stitches an extra panel. Rome’s system divides the coat — grace infused, merit added, satisfaction paid, purgatory finishing the hem. The gospel says the robe comes whole, from above, woven from the top throughout, and is put upon the sinner by faith alone. A patched righteousness is no righteousness; it is a rag with a good lining.
roots_summary: One who interlaces warp and woof; his shuttle measures life and his loom clothes Christ.
roots_lines: Weaver — Old English wefan, to weave, akin to German weben.
Warp = the stretched threads; woof = the thread the shuttle carries across.
Job’s days fly swifter than a weaver’s shuttle (Job 7:6).
Hezekiah’s life is cut from the loom in the midst of the pattern (Isa 38:12).
The Lord’s coat was seamless, woven from the top throughout (Joh 19:23).
usage: Swifter than a weaver’s shuttle — the oldest and truest measure of a man’s days.
God holds the shears; the web comes off the beam at His word, not ours.
A seamless coat cannot be divided, and neither can the righteousness it pictures.

etymology: From the Old French embrouder, “to ornament with needlework” (en-, “in,” + brouder, “to stitch,” of Frankish origin); hence one who works figures and colours into cloth with the needle.
biblical_def: An embroiderer works coloured thread into finished cloth with the needle — the “needlework” of the Authorized Version. He is one of the few craftsmen in Scripture whose skill is expressly traced to the Holy Ghost. For the tabernacle the LORD called Bezaleel by name (Exo 31:2) and said, “I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship” (Exo 31:3), and gave him Aholiab, who was “an engraver, and a cunning workman, and an embroiderer in blue, and in purple, and in scarlet, and fine linen” (Exo 38:23). Moses records the same of the whole company: “them hath he filled with wisdom of heart, to work all manner of work, of the engraver, and of the cunning workman, and of the embroiderer” (Exo 35:35). Two truths sit together here and neither may be let go. The first is that artistic skill is a gift of God, not a merely natural talent, and the embroiderer’s needle is as truly Spirit-given as the prophet’s tongue. The second is that this gift was never turned loose. Every colour, measure, and figure was commanded; the workmen wrought “according to all that the LORD had commanded” (Exo 36:1). Beauty in the worship of God is not optional and it is not free. It is prescribed.
webster_summary: One who embroiders; a worker of figures and colours into cloth with the needle.
webster_full: EMBROIDERER, one who embroiders; a worker of ornamental figures upon cloth with the needle.
From Old French embrouder, to ornament with needlework.
The Authorized Version usually calls the product needlework.
Aholiab of the tribe of Dan was an embroiderer in blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen (Exo 38:23).
Their skill is expressly ascribed to the spirit of God (Exo 31:3; Exo 35:35).
scriptures: Exo 31:3
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,
Exo 36:1

Then wrought Bezaleel and Aholiab, and every wise hearted man, in whom the LORD put wisdom and understanding to know how to work all manner of work for the service of the sanctuary, according to all that the LORD had commanded.
And to devise curious works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass,
Syria was thy merchant by reason of the multitude of the wares of thy making: they occupied in thy fairs with emeralds, purple, and broidered work, and fine linen, and coral, and agate.
corruption_summary: Spirit-given artistry, held under the LORD's own pattern — the regulative principle applied to beauty.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions meet at the embroiderer’s frame. The first is the bare and joyless instinct that treats beauty in the house of God as worldliness, as if the Lord who commanded blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen were indifferent to loveliness. He is not. He named the artist, filled him with His Spirit, and specified the colours. The second corruption is the modern worship industry, which has taken the artist’s gift and cut it loose from the command — the service designed for effect, the lighting and staging tuned to produce a feeling, the platform run on the logic of performance. The tabernacle answers both. Its beauty was extravagant, and every thread of it was prescribed. Bezaleel had immense freedom of hand within an absolute boundary of command, and that is precisely what the regulative principle protects: not ugliness, but obedience.

There is a further word here about the ordinary Christian craftswoman and craftsman. Exodus 35 does not say the LORD filled Bezaleel with wisdom to preach; it says He filled him to work in gold, in blue, in purple, and with the needle. The Spirit’s gifting is not confined to the pulpit. A woman who sews well, a man who cuts a joint true, a hand that makes a plain thing beautiful — these are gifts of the same Giver, and they are to be offered back to Him with the same reverence. The world tells such workers that their skill is self-expression. Scripture tells them it is stewardship, given by God, to be used at His direction and for His glory.
roots_summary: A worker of needlework; the Spirit-filled artisan of the tabernacle, free in hand and bound by command.
roots_lines: Embroiderer — Old French embrouder, to ornament with the needle.
The AV renders the product needlework and broidered work.
Bezaleel was called by name and filled with the spirit of God (Exo 31:2–3).
Aholiab of Dan was an embroiderer in blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen (Exo 38:23).
All was wrought according to all that the LORD had commanded (Exo 36:1).
usage: The tabernacle’s embroiderer was Spirit-filled and pattern-bound at once.
Beauty in worship is commanded, not invented.
Skill in the hands is a gift of God and a stewardship, never mere self-expression.

etymology: From the Latin apotheca, “a storehouse,” from the Greek apothēkē (apo-, “away,” + tithēmi, “to put”); hence a keeper of a store of spices and drugs, a compounder of ointments and perfumes.
biblical_def: An apothecary is the compounder of ointments, perfumes, and spices — the confectioner of the ancient world, master of proportion and heat. The Authorized Version gives him an astonishing dignity: he is the pattern for the making of the two holiest compounds in Israel. Of the anointing oil the LORD says, “thou shalt make it an oil of holy ointment, an ointment compound after the art of the apothecary: it shall be an holy anointing oil” (Exo 30:25); and of the incense, “thou shalt make it a perfume, a confection after the art of the apothecary, tempered together, pure and holy” (Exo 30:35). The obedience is recorded in the same terms: Bezaleel “made the holy anointing oil, and the pure incense of sweet spices, according to the work of the apothecary” (Exo 37:29). Yet the same book forbids any man to compound the like for himself, on pain of being cut off — the art was licensed only for the LORD’s use. Then Solomon takes the trade and makes it a proverb that has never been improved upon: “Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour” (Ecc 10:1). Months of skill and a fortune in spices, ruined by a fly. So a lifetime’s reputation is ruined by one folly.
webster_summary: One who prepares and compounds drugs, spices, ointments, and perfumes; the ancient confectioner of holy oil.
webster_full: APOTHECARY, one who prepares and sells drugs and medicines; a compounder of ointments and perfumes.
From Latin apotheca, a storehouse, from Greek apothēkē, a place of putting away.
The holy anointing oil was compounded “after the art of the apothecary” (Exo 30:25).
So was the incense — a confection tempered together, pure and holy (Exo 30:35).
Solomon’s proverb: dead flies spoil the apothecary’s ointment (Ecc 10:1).
scriptures: And thou shalt make it an oil of holy ointment, an ointment compound after the art of the apothecary: it shall be an holy anointing oil.
And thou shalt make it a perfume, a confection after the art of the apothecary, tempered together, pure and holy:
And he made the holy anointing oil, and the pure incense of sweet spices, according to the work of the apothecary.
Ecc 10:1
Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour.
corruption_summary: A little folly outweighs much wisdom — and a trade licensed for holy use is a warning against unauthorised worship.
corruption_paragraphs: Ecclesiastes 10:1 is a doctrine of reputation the modern church badly needs. The arithmetic is not proportional but catastrophic: a small quantity of corruption spoils a large quantity of good, because the nature of the whole is changed. A single fly does not make the ointment ninety-nine per cent fragrant; it makes the jar stink. So a pastor of thirty faithful years is remembered for one covered-over sin; so a testimony built slowly is undone in an evening. The world calls this unfair. Scripture calls it the way ointment works. The application is neither despair nor cynicism but watchfulness — guard the small things, since it is the small things that carry the smell.

The second warning is about unauthorised compounding. The holy oil and the holy incense were given by exact recipe and reserved for the LORD alone; whoever made the like for common use was to be cut off from his people. God does not merely command that He be worshipped; He commands how, and He guards the how with penalties. Nadab and Abihu learned it with strange fire (Lev 10:1). The apothecary’s art therefore stands as one of the plainest Old Testament footings of the regulative principle: even the perfume of the sanctuary was not left to a craftsman’s taste. Where God has spoken to the manner of His worship, invention is not creativity but trespass.
roots_summary: A compounder of spices and ointments; the LORD's own pattern for the holy oil and the incense.
roots_lines: Apothecary — Latin apotheca, a storehouse; Greek apothēkē.
The Hebrew raqach means to compound or perfume; hence a confectioner of spices.
The holy anointing oil was made after his art (Exo 30:25).
So was the incense, tempered together, pure and holy (Exo 30:35).
Dead flies in his ointment picture a little folly in a good name (Ecc 10:1).
usage: After the art of the apothecary — the LORD prescribed even the perfume of His house.
Dead flies cause the ointment to stink: a little folly ruins a long reputation.
The recipe was licensed for holy use only; imitation was trespass, not craftsmanship.
